questions.q: What do we call a line that divides an object into two identical mirror images?
questions.a: This is called a line of symmetry. A wrong answer here suggests the student is confusing "symmetry" with "balance" or "similarity" without understanding the specific geometric requirement of reflection.

questions.q: If a sunflower looks the same after being rotated by 90 degrees, does it possess symmetry? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: Yes, it possesses rotational symmetry because it repeats its appearance before a full 360-degree turn. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks symmetry *only* means a mirror line (reflection), ignoring that repetition through rotation also counts.

questions.q: A starfish has five arms arranged around a center. If you rotate it, how many times will it look identical to its starting position before completing a full circle?
questions.a: It will look identical 5 times (including the final 360-degree position). A student might incorrectly guess 4 or 6, revealing they haven't counted the "arms" as the repeating units of the pattern.

questions.q: Compare the symmetry of a cloud to that of a butterfly. Why is one considered symmetrical and the other not?
questions.a: A butterfly has a definite, repeating pattern (reflectional), whereas a cloud has no fixed, repeating structure. If a student says both are "random," they have failed to identify the concept of a "definite pattern" as the core of symmetry.

questions.q: Is it possible for a natural object to have rotational symmetry but NO line of symmetry? Give an example.
questions.a: Yes, an example is a pinwheel-like flower or a spiral shell. A student might argue "no" because they are stuck on the idea that symmetry must be a "mirror fold," failing to distinguish between reflection and rotation.

questions.q: Design a simple leaf or flower pattern that has exactly two lines of symmetry. How would you draw it?
questions.a: The student should describe a cross-like or oval-like shape where you can fold it vertically and horizontally. An answer that draws a circle (infinite lines) or a triangle (3 lines) shows they haven't grasped the specific constraint of "exactly two."
